newsitem.title: USA: Kessler to leave post as FDA chief in early 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kessler to leave post as FDA chief in early 1997.

text.p: Food and Drug Commissioner David Kessler, leader of the Clinton Administration's fight to regulate tobacco, will leave his post in early 1997 when a successor has been named, FDA officials said Monday.
They said he had been asked by President Clinton to stay on as the nation's top food and drug safety official, and that he agreed, but only until a replacement was appointed.
Kessler, a doctor and lawyer, was named to the post by President George Bush in 1990 and Clinton asked him to remain in the high profile -- and controversial -- job.
The FDA chief said in a statement that he appreciated the opportunity to serve the public but now believes "it is time to return to private life."

President Clinton praised Kessler's "tireless commitment" to public service and said "his contributions to improve the health of our nation are many and their effect will continue to be felt for generations to come."

Kessler's last years were embroiled in controversy, not only for his moves to curb cigarette smoking, especially by children, but also from a new Republican-controlled Congress that fought to reduce FDA oversight of the drug industry.
